title: Machine Learning Basics
tagline: Teaching machines to learn from data rather than programming every rule by hand.

sections.content:
Machine learning (ML) is a subfield of artificial intelligence where systems **learn patterns from data** rather than following a fixed set of hand-written rules. The key shift in thinking is this: instead of a programmer writing `if temperature > 30 then classify as hot`, you collect thousands of labelled weather observations and let the algorithm discover the boundary itself. The program that results is not a list of if-statements — it is a mathematical function whose internal parameters were shaped by data.

This idea is deceptively simple, yet it underlies almost every technology trend of the last decade: image recognition, language translation, recommendation engines, fraud detection, protein folding, and the large language models that power modern AI assistants. Understanding what ML is — and equally what it is **not** — is therefore essential for any software engineer working in the modern era.

There are three main paradigms that organise nearly all of ML. **Supervised learning** trains on labelled input-output pairs (images tagged cat/dog, emails tagged spam/not-spam) and learns a mapping function from inputs to outputs. **Unsupervised learning** finds hidden structure in unlabelled data — grouping customers by purchasing behaviour, compressing images, or generating new examples. **Reinforcement learning** trains an agent by rewarding desirable actions and penalising bad ones, as in training a game-playing bot through millions of rounds of trial and error.

This chapter builds the conceptual foundation you need to reason about any ML system: the vocabulary of **features**, **labels**, **training and test splits**, **overfitting vs. underfitting**, **loss functions**, and **gradient descent**. We will work through concrete worked examples in JavaScript to make the mathematics tangible, and we will explore the important edge cases and misconceptions that trip up beginners and experienced engineers alike.

sections.title: Teaching a Child to Recognise Cats
sections.content:
**Supervised learning** is like teaching a child to identify cats. You sit with them and flip through hundreds of photos, saying 'cat' or 'not a cat' for each one. The child's brain gradually builds an internal model — adjusting which features matter (pointy ears, whiskers, fur texture, body shape) and which do not (background colour, photo orientation). After enough labelled examples, the child can correctly classify a cat they have never seen before. You never spelled out a rule; the rule emerged from examples.

**Unsupervised learning** removes the teacher. You hand the child a box of five hundred mixed animal photos with no labels at all. Left alone, they spontaneously sort the pile — the fluffy ones here, the scaly ones there, the ones with feathers in a third pile. The groupings they form may or may not align with scientific taxonomy, but they are real structure found without guidance.

**Reinforcement learning** is like training a dog with treats. The dog tries an action; if it is the right action it gets a treat (positive reward), otherwise nothing — or a mild correction (negative reward). Over hundreds of repetitions the dog learns to perform the trick without anyone explaining *how* to do it. The policy — the mapping from situation to action — is discovered entirely through interaction and reward signals. This is how AlphaGo learned to play Go at superhuman level and how RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) fine-tunes large language models to follow instructions.

sections.title: Features and Labels: The Vocabulary of Data
sections.content:
Every ML model operates on structured representations of the world. A **feature** is a measurable input variable: house square footage, the number of exclamation marks in an email, the pixel intensity at position (x, y) in an image, the frequency of the word 'free' in a document. Features are the raw signals the model has access to.

A **label** (or target) is the output you want to predict. House price (a continuous number — a **regression** problem). Spam or not-spam (a discrete category — a **classification** problem). The rating a user will give a movie they have not yet seen (a recommendation problem that can be framed as regression).

In supervised learning, your dataset is a collection of (features, label) pairs: `[(x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), ..., (xₙ, yₙ)]`. The model learns a function `f` such that `f(xᵢ) ≈ yᵢ`. During inference (deployment), new inputs arrive without labels, and the model predicts the label from features alone.

**Feature engineering** — the art of choosing and transforming the right features — is often the most important determinant of model performance, more important than the choice of algorithm. A brilliant algorithm fed useless features will fail; a simple linear model given the right features can outperform a deep neural network. This is captured in the phrase: 'garbage in, garbage out.' Real-world features often need normalisation (scaling to zero mean, unit variance), handling of missing values, encoding of categorical variables (one-hot encoding), and careful construction of interaction terms.

sections.title: Train, Validation, and Test Splits: Honest Evaluation
sections.content:
The single most important discipline in applied ML is **never evaluating a model on data it trained on**. If you do, you get an optimistic, meaningless number. The model may have memorised the training examples rather than learning anything generalisable.

The standard practice is to **split your dataset before any training begins**. A typical split for medium datasets is 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test. Smaller datasets often use 80/20 train/test, with **k-fold cross-validation** to get reliable estimates from limited data.

The **training set** is what the model actually learns from — gradient descent runs on this data. The **validation set** (also called development set) is held out from training and used to evaluate the model during development: choosing between model architectures, tuning hyperparameters (learning rate, number of layers, regularisation strength), and deciding when to stop training. The **test set** is touched exactly once, at the very end, to report the final performance of the fully trained and tuned model.

Why the strict separation? If you use the test set to guide any decisions — even something as small as 'let me try a larger model and check if the test accuracy improves' — you have inadvertently **overfitted to the test set**. It is no longer a fair holdout. This is a subtle but pervasive mistake in published ML research and in industry practice.

**k-fold cross-validation** is an elegant solution when data is scarce. You divide the training set into k equal folds (typically k=5 or k=10). You train k separate models, each time using k-1 folds for training and the remaining fold for validation. The k validation scores are averaged for a low-variance performance estimate. Every example ends up in the validation fold exactly once — maximum data usage.

sections.title: Overfitting and Underfitting: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
sections.content:
**Overfitting** is what happens when a model learns the training data too well — it memorises noise and quirks rather than the underlying pattern. A decision tree grown to full depth, with one leaf per training example, will classify every training point perfectly yet perform no better than random guessing on new data. Signs of overfitting: training accuracy near 100%, test accuracy significantly lower.

**Underfitting** is the opposite: the model is too simple to capture the real structure in the data. A linear model forced onto obviously curved data will have high error on both training and test sets. Signs of underfitting: both training and test error are high.

This is the classic **bias-variance tradeoff**. A high-bias model (too simple) systematically misses patterns — it underfits. A high-variance model (too complex) chases random fluctuations in training data — it overfits. The goal is a model complex enough to capture the signal, but regularised enough to ignore the noise.

**Remedies for overfitting:**
- **More training data** — the most reliable cure. More data gives the model less opportunity to memorise noise.
- **L1/L2 regularisation** — add a penalty term to the loss function that discourages large weight values. L2 (weight decay) pulls weights toward zero smoothly; L1 (lasso) pushes many weights exactly to zero, producing sparse models.
- **Dropout** (for neural networks) — randomly zero out a fraction of neuron activations during training. Each mini-batch trains a slightly different sub-network, producing an ensemble effect.
- **Early stopping** — monitor validation loss during training and stop when it stops improving. Training loss continues falling, but validation loss is your true signal.
- **Simpler model** — fewer parameters, shallower trees, lower-degree polynomials.

**Remedies for underfitting:**
- Add more features or engineer better features.
- Increase model complexity (more layers, more trees, higher polynomial degree).
- Train for more epochs.
- Reduce regularisation strength.

sections.title: Loss Functions: Measuring How Wrong the Model Is
sections.content:
Before a model can learn, you need a **loss function** (also called cost function or objective function) that measures, in a single number, how badly the model is currently performing. Gradient descent then minimises this number by adjusting parameters.

**Mean Squared Error (MSE)** is the standard loss for regression:
`MSE = (1/n) Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²`
where `yᵢ` is the true label and `ŷᵢ` is the model's prediction. Squaring the errors penalises large mistakes heavily and ensures all contributions are positive.

**Binary Cross-Entropy** is the standard loss for binary classification (spam/not-spam):
`Loss = -(1/n) Σ [yᵢ log(ŷᵢ) + (1-yᵢ) log(1-ŷᵢ)]`
This measures the dissimilarity between the model's predicted probability distribution and the true distribution. A perfect classifier that always outputs probability 1.0 for the correct class has zero cross-entropy loss.

**Why squared error, not absolute error?** MSE is differentiable everywhere, making gradient computation straightforward. Mean Absolute Error (MAE) has a subgradient at zero and is more robust to outliers but slightly harder to optimise. In practice, MSE is the default; MAE or Huber loss is used when the target variable has heavy-tailed outliers.

The loss function is not just a technical detail — it encodes **what the model is optimising for**. Train with the wrong loss and the model learns the wrong behaviour, even if training proceeds without error. For instance, using accuracy as a loss function directly is problematic because accuracy is not differentiable — you cannot compute its gradient to steer gradient descent.

sections.title: Gradient Descent: The Engine of Learning
sections.content:
**Gradient descent** is the iterative optimisation algorithm that adjusts a model's parameters to reduce the loss function. It is the workhorse of almost all modern ML, from simple linear regression to GPT-4.

Here is the core intuition: imagine the loss function as a hilly landscape, with the model's current parameters defining a point on that landscape. The loss is the altitude. You want to reach the lowest valley. At any point, the **gradient** of the loss with respect to the parameters tells you the direction of steepest uphill. By taking a step in the **opposite** direction — downhill — you lower the loss. Repeat thousands or millions of times, and you converge to a minimum.

The update rule for each parameter W is:
`W ← W - α × (∂Loss/∂W)`

where `α` (alpha) is the **learning rate** — a hyperparameter that controls step size.

**Choosing the learning rate is critical.** Too large: the steps overshoot minima, causing oscillation or divergence. Too small: convergence is extremely slow, and you may get stuck in a local flat region. Modern practice uses **adaptive optimisers** like Adam, which maintain per-parameter learning rates that automatically scale based on the history of gradients — eliminating most of the sensitivity to the initial learning rate choice.

**Variants of gradient descent** differ in how much data they process before each update:
- **Batch gradient descent** computes the gradient over the entire training set before each step. Very accurate gradients but extremely slow on large datasets.
- **Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)** updates parameters after every single example. Fast but noisy — the gradient estimate is high-variance.
- **Mini-batch gradient descent** (the standard) uses a random subset of 32–512 examples per step. Balances the accuracy of batch with the speed of SGD, and is efficient on GPU hardware.

**The loss landscape for deep neural networks** is non-convex — it has many local minima and saddle points, not a single global minimum. Surprisingly, this is less of a problem than it sounds: in high-dimensional spaces, most local minima have similar loss values to the global minimum. Saddle points (where gradient is zero but it is not a minimum) are more common and gradient noise from mini-batching helps escape them.

flowchart TD
  A["Initialise params W randomly"] --> B["Forward Pass\ncompute prediction"]
  B --> C["Compute Loss\nMSE or cross-entropy"]
  C --> D["Backward Pass\ncompute gradients"]
  D --> E["Update: W = W - lr * grad"]
  E --> F{"Converged?"}
  F -->|"No"| B
  F -->|"Yes"| G["Trained Model"]
sections.caption: The gradient descent training loop. Each iteration is called an 'epoch' for full-batch, or a 'step' for mini-batch. Convergence is detected by watching the validation loss plateau.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The loop computes the MSE gradient analytically: dLoss/dw = (2/n) * Σ (ŷᵢ - yᵢ) * xᵢ and dLoss/db = (2/n) * Σ (ŷᵢ - yᵢ). Each epoch updates both parameters by stepping opposite to their gradients. After 2000 epochs the parameters converge close to the true relationship (≈ 2x + 0). Comparing train vs. test MSE is a direct overfitting diagnostic — a large gap means the model is not generalising.

sections.title: A Tour of Common Algorithms
sections.content:
**Linear regression** fits a weighted sum of features to a continuous target. It is interpretable, fast, and works remarkably well when the relationship is approximately linear. Each weight directly tells you 'increasing this feature by 1 unit changes the prediction by this much.'

**Logistic regression** applies a sigmoid function to the linear combination to produce a probability between 0 and 1. Despite the name, it is a classification algorithm. It is the workhorse of industry classification tasks where interpretability matters (credit scoring, medical risk).

**Decision trees** recursively split the feature space with axis-aligned cuts ('is age > 35? is income < $50k?'). Extremely interpretable and handle categorical features naturally. Prone to overfitting when grown deep. **Random forests** ensemble hundreds of trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample with a random subset of features, and average their predictions — dramatically reducing variance with little increase in bias.

**Support Vector Machines (SVMs)** find the maximum-margin hyperplane separating two classes. The 'kernel trick' allows SVMs to work in high-dimensional implicit feature spaces, making them powerful for text classification and bioinformatics. Now largely replaced by neural networks for tasks with abundant data.

**Neural networks** stack layers of linear transformations interleaved with non-linear activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh). Each layer learns an increasingly abstract representation of the input. With enough layers and data, neural networks can approximate any continuous function — the theoretical basis is the **universal approximation theorem**. Deep neural networks power image recognition (CNNs), natural language processing (Transformers), and generative AI.

**k-Means clustering** (unsupervised) assigns each example to one of k clusters by iteratively computing cluster centroids and reassigning examples to their nearest centroid. Simple and fast, but requires choosing k in advance and assumes spherical clusters of similar size.

**Principal Component Analysis (PCA)** (unsupervised) finds the directions of maximum variance in the data and projects onto those directions, reducing dimensionality while preserving as much information as possible.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: k-NN perfectly illustrates the bias-variance tradeoff: k=1 overfits (zero training error, high variance); k=N underfits (ignores local structure). The right k is a hyperparameter tuned on the validation set, not the test set. Notice there are no parameters to update during 'training' — all computation is deferred to prediction time, making k-NN a lazy learner with O(n) prediction cost.

sections.title: Evaluation Metrics: Beyond Accuracy
sections.content:
**Accuracy** (fraction of correctly classified examples) is the default intuition for classification, but it is dangerously misleading on **imbalanced datasets**. If 99% of emails are not spam, a model that always predicts 'not spam' achieves 99% accuracy while being completely useless.

**Precision** = TP / (TP + FP) — of everything the model called positive, what fraction actually was? High precision means few false alarms.

**Recall** (sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN) — of everything that actually is positive, what fraction did the model catch? High recall means few misses.

The **F1 score** = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall) is the harmonic mean, balancing both concerns. It is the go-to metric when classes are imbalanced.

**ROC-AUC** (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) measures how well the model separates two classes across all possible decision thresholds. An AUC of 0.5 is random; 1.0 is perfect. AUC is threshold-independent, making it useful for comparing models before choosing an operating point.

**For regression:** beyond MSE, **Mean Absolute Error (MAE)** is more interpretable ('on average off by X units') and **R² (coefficient of determination)** measures the fraction of variance in the target explained by the model (1.0 = perfect, 0.0 = no better than predicting the mean).

A crucial practical lesson: **choose the evaluation metric before you begin**. The metric should match the business problem. In medical screening for a rare cancer, recall (catching all true positives) matters far more than precision. In a spam filter for a CEO, precision (avoiding false positives) may matter more than recall.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The confusion matrix (TP, FP, TN, FN) is the foundation for all classification metrics. Precision and recall trade off against each other — lowering the classification threshold increases recall but decreases precision. F1 is the balanced summary. Notice that a model with 95% accuracy can have 0% recall on the minority class — accuracy is misleading when classes are skewed.

sections.content: **A brief history:** The term 'machine learning' was coined by Arthur Samuel in 1959, who built a self-improving checkers program at IBM. The field exploded in the 2010s when deep learning (neural networks with many layers, trained on GPUs with massive datasets) dramatically outperformed previous approaches on image recognition (AlexNet, 2012), speech recognition, and natural language processing. The Transformer architecture (Google, 2017) — 'Attention Is All You Need' — is the architectural foundation for GPT, BERT, and virtually every modern large language model. The defining resource shift: data and compute now matter more than algorithmic cleverness for many tasks.

**Common mistakes and interview traps:**

- **Evaluating on training data** is the single most common beginner error. Always hold out a test set before any training begins, and touch it exactly once.
- **Data leakage** — when information from the test set inadvertently influences training. Classic examples: normalising features using statistics computed over the full dataset (including test), or including future information in features when predicting the past. Leakage causes optimistic metrics that collapse in production.
- **Confusing the number of values with the maximum value** does not apply here — but do not confuse **accuracy** with **model quality** on imbalanced data.
- **Learning rate is the most sensitive hyperparameter** in neural network training. If your loss is not decreasing, try a learning rate 10x smaller. If it oscillates wildly, try 10x smaller still.
- **Gradient descent finds a local minimum**, not necessarily the global one. For convex problems (linear regression, logistic regression) there is only one minimum — gradient descent is guaranteed to find it. For deep neural networks the landscape is non-convex, but empirically this is usually fine.
- **More data almost always beats a better algorithm** at a fixed compute budget. When stuck, ask: can I get more labelled examples?

items: **Supervised learning** trains on labelled (features, label) pairs; **unsupervised learning** finds structure in unlabelled data; **reinforcement learning** learns by maximising cumulative reward through interaction. These three paradigms cover almost all practical ML.

**Features** are measurable input variables; **labels** are target outputs. Feature engineering — selecting and transforming the right inputs — is often the single largest lever for improving model performance.

**Train/validation/test split** enforces honest evaluation. Train on training data, tune hyperparameters on validation data, and touch the test set exactly once for the final unbiased performance estimate.

**Overfitting** = low training error, high test error — the model memorised noise. Fix with more data, regularisation (L1/L2), dropout, or early stopping. **Underfitting** = high error everywhere — the model is too simple; increase complexity or engineer better features.

**Gradient descent** iteratively moves model parameters in the direction that reduces the loss function. The update rule `W ← W - α × gradient` is the foundation of training for linear models, SVMs, and deep neural networks alike.

**Accuracy is not enough.** On imbalanced datasets, precision, recall, F1, and AUC are essential. Choose your evaluation metric before training begins, based on the business cost of false positives vs. false negatives.

**k-NN illustrates bias-variance tradeoff** concretely: k=1 overfits, k=N underfits, and the optimal k is found via validation set — the same principle applies to every algorithm's complexity hyperparameters.

quiz.question: Which ML paradigm trains on labelled (input, output) pairs to learn a mapping function?
options: Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning
Self-supervised learning
quiz.explanation: Supervised learning uses labelled examples where each input has a corresponding correct output. The model learns to map inputs to outputs. Unsupervised learning uses no labels; reinforcement learning uses a reward signal rather than labelled pairs; self-supervised learning generates its own labels from the data structure.

quiz.question: What does 'overfitting' mean in machine learning?
options: The model is too simple and has high error on both training and test data
The model performs well on training data but poorly on unseen test data
The model was trained for too many epochs and the weights overflow
The training dataset is much larger than necessary
quiz.explanation: Overfitting means the model has memorised the training data — including its noise — rather than learning generalisable patterns. Training accuracy is high but test accuracy is much lower. The opposite failure mode (too-simple model, high error everywhere) is underfitting.

quiz.question: Why must the test set be held out and touched only once, at the very end?
options: To reduce training time by using less data
To provide an unbiased estimate of real-world performance on data the model has never influenced
To allow the model to train on harder examples last
To comply with data privacy regulations
quiz.explanation: Any model decision informed by the test set — even indirectly — causes the test set to overestimate real performance. A held-out test set that is never touched during training or hyperparameter tuning gives an honest estimate of how the model generalises to new, unseen data.

quiz.question: In the gradient descent update rule W = W - lr * (dLoss/dW), what does the negative sign achieve?
options: It converts maximisation into minimisation of the number of parameters
It moves parameters in the direction that decreases the loss — opposite to the gradient
It normalises the gradient to unit length before applying the update
It prevents the parameters from ever becoming negative values
quiz.explanation: The gradient points in the direction of steepest *increase* of the loss. Subtracting the gradient (stepping in the opposite direction) decreases the loss. This is why the algorithm is called gradient *descent* — you descend the loss surface. Without the negative sign you would perform gradient ascent and maximise the loss.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of unsupervised learning?
options: Classifying emails as spam or not-spam using labelled examples
Training a robot arm to assemble parts using a reward signal
Grouping customers by purchasing behaviour without predefined category labels
Predicting house prices from historical labelled sales data
quiz.explanation: Grouping customers without predefined labels is clustering — a classic unsupervised learning task. The algorithm finds structure in data without being told what categories exist. Spam classification and price prediction are supervised (labelled pairs); robot training with a reward signal is reinforcement learning.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a validation set, distinct from the test set?
options: To train the model faster by providing easier examples first
To tune hyperparameters during development without contaminating the final test evaluation
To replace the test set when labelled data is scarce
To store model checkpoints between training runs
quiz.explanation: If you use the test set to choose hyperparameters (learning rate, model depth, regularisation), you overfit to it and lose its unbiased nature. The validation set is used during development for all tuning decisions. The test set is reserved for one final honest evaluation after all design choices are frozen.

quiz.question: On a dataset where 98% of examples are class A and 2% are class B, a model that always predicts class A achieves 98% accuracy. What metric best exposes this problem?
options: Training loss
Mean squared error on the test set
Recall (sensitivity) for class B
Number of training epochs
quiz.explanation: Recall for the minority class B = TP / (TP + FN). A model that always predicts A never correctly identifies any class B examples, so recall for B = 0%. This immediately exposes the failure that 98% accuracy hides. F1 score (harmonic mean of precision and recall) and AUC are similarly useful on imbalanced datasets.

quiz.question: In k-nearest neighbours, what happens as k increases from 1 to the full training set size N?
options: The model moves from underfitting to overfitting
The model moves from overfitting (k=1) to underfitting (k=N)
Prediction accuracy always improves as k grows
The training time grows but the prediction time stays constant
quiz.explanation: k=1 is maximum variance — every noisy point influences predictions, and training accuracy is 100% (a point is its own nearest neighbour). As k grows, more neighbours vote and local noise is smoothed out, reducing variance. At k=N every point votes and the prediction is always the majority class — the model has collapsed to a constant, underfitting completely.

quiz.question: Which remedy is most directly targeted at overfitting caused by a model that is too complex relative to the amount of training data?
options: Increasing the learning rate to converge faster
Gathering more training data or adding L2 regularisation
Removing examples from the test set
Increasing the number of training epochs
quiz.explanation: Overfitting reflects excess model capacity relative to data. More data gives the model less opportunity to memorise noise. L2 regularisation penalises large weights, discouraging the extreme curve-fitting that causes overfitting. Increasing epochs makes overfitting worse; removing test examples is invalid and does not help generalisation.

quiz.question: What is 'data leakage' in a machine learning pipeline?
options: Training data accidentally being deleted from disk during preprocessing
Information from the test or future data inadvertently influencing the training process, causing inflated metrics
A model architecture with too many parameters relative to the dataset size
The gradient becoming very small during backpropagation, slowing learning
quiz.explanation: Data leakage occurs when information that would not be available at real prediction time — including test set statistics or future observations — influences model training or feature construction. Classic examples: computing normalisation statistics over the full dataset before splitting, or including future prices in features for a stock prediction model. Leakage produces optimistic metrics that collapse when the model is deployed.
